Implementing the BYM2 Model in Stan

The BYM2 Model: Riebler et al, 2016

The ICAR model assumes complete spatial correlation between regions. This simplifying assumption makes it cheap to compute; the CAR model, which adds a weight to each neighbor pair to account for the strength of the spatial correlation, requires computing the inverse of the adjacency matrix, an cubic operation. For maps with more than a handful of regions, this is prohibitively expensive, computationally. The Besag York Mollié (BYM) model was developed to address this problem; the BYM2 model builds on this model and subsequent refinements.

  • Poisson regression + component for extra variation which combines spatial and non-spatial components \(\phi + \theta\) as \[\left( (\sqrt{\, {\rho} / s}\, \ )\,\phi^* + (\sqrt{1-\rho})\,\theta^* \right) \sigma \] where:

    • \(\sigma\geq 0\) is the overall standard deviation.
    • \(\rho \in [0,1]\) - proportion of spatial variance.
    • \(\phi^*\) is the ICAR component.
    • \(\theta^* \sim N(0, 1)\) is the vector of ordinary random effects
    • \(s\) is a scaling factor s.t. \(\operatorname{Var}(\phi_i) \approx 1\); \(s\) is data.

  • Follows previous BYM modifications, notably Leroux 2000, which has a single scale parameter plus mixing parameter.

  • Adds a scaling factor on the ICAR component so that for each element \(i\) in vectors \(\theta\) and \(\phi\), \(\operatorname{Var}(\theta_i) \approx \operatorname{Var}(\phi_i) \approx 1\). The scaling factor is derived from the adjacency matrix (neighbors graph).

New York City Neighbor Graph

New York city consists of several islands; only the Bronx is part of the mainland; Brooklyn and Queens are part of Long Island, plus smaller islands City Island, Roosevelt Island, and the Rockaways.

This is a problem for the ICAR model, which operates on a fully connected graph (single component)

print(f'mean number of neighbors per node: {w_nyc_nbs.mean_neighbors}')

From ICAR to BYM2

  • The BYM2 model combines both ICAR component \(\phi\) and ordinary random effects \(\theta\) as \[\left( (\sqrt{\, {\rho} / s}\, \ )\,\phi^* + (\sqrt{1-\rho})\,\theta^* \right) \sigma \]

  • Parameter \(\rho\) answers the question: how much of the observed variance is spatial?

  • Don’t need to run analysis, e.g. Moran’s I - the model sorts it out for you.

BYM2 Model: bym2.stan

This file is in directory stan/bym2.stan.

Python

bym2_model_file = os.path.join('stan', 'bym2.stan')

with open(bym2_model_file, 'r') as file:
    contents = file.read()
    print(contents)

R

bym2_model_file = file.path('stan', 'bym2.stan')
cat(readLines(bym2_model_file), sep="\n")
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  array[N] int<lower=0> y; // count outcomes
  vector<lower=0>[N] E; // exposure
  int<lower=1> K; // num covariates
  matrix[N, K] xs; // design matrix

  // spatial structure
  int<lower = 0> N_edges;  // number of neighbor pairs
  array[2, N_edges] int<lower = 1, upper = N> neighbors;  // columnwise adjacent

  real tau; // scaling factor
}
transformed data {
  vector[N] log_E = log(E);
  // center continuous predictors 
  vector[K] means_xs;  // column means of xs before centering
  matrix[N, K] xs_centered;  // centered version of xs
  for (k in 1:K) {
    means_xs[k] = mean(xs[, k]);
    xs_centered[, k] = xs[, k] - means_xs[k];
  }
}
parameters {
  real beta0; // intercept
  vector[K] betas; // covariates
  real<lower=0, upper=1> rho; // proportion of spatial variance
  sum_to_zero_vector[N] phi;  // spatial effects
  vector[N] theta; // heterogeneous random effects
  real<lower = 0> sigma;  // scale of combined effects
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] gamma = sqrt(1 - rho) * theta + sqrt(rho * inv(tau)) * phi;  // BYM2
}
model {
  y ~ poisson_log(log_E + beta0 + xs_centered * betas + gamma * sigma);
  rho ~ beta(0.5, 0.5);
  target += -0.5 * dot_self(phi[neighbors[1]] - phi[neighbors[2]]); // ICAR prior
  beta0 ~ std_normal();
  betas ~ std_normal();
  theta ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ std_normal();
}
generated quantities {
  real beta_intercept = beta0 - dot_product(means_xs, betas);  // adjust intercept
  array[N] int y_rep;
  {
    vector[N] eta = log_E + beta0 + xs_centered * betas + gamma * sigma;
    y_rep = max(eta) < 26 ? poisson_log_rng(eta) : rep_array(-1, N);
  }
}

Compute scaling factor tau

The BYM2 model component gamma combines an vector of non-spatial random effects theta, and the vector of spatial random effects phi. The prior on theta is std_normal() thus the its variance is approximately \(1\). The prior on phi is the ICAR component, the spatial covariance matrix. To make the variance of the phi be approximately \(1\), Riebler et. al. recommend scaling it by the geometric mean of the variance of the spatial adjacency matrix. This quantity is tau, and is computed by helper function get_scaling_factor.

Python

tau = get_scaling_factor(brooklyn_nbs)
tau

R

tau = get_scaling_factor(brooklyn_nbs)
tau
[1] 0.5082443

Workflow: Prior Predictive Checking

Prior and posterior predictive checks are two cases of the general concept of predictive checks, just conditioning on different things (no data and the observed data, respectively). Posteior predictive checks were introduced in the Stan model building workflow notebook, which shows how to generate a new dataset (y_rep) in the generated quantities block based on the sample estimate of the model parameters. Comparison of the replicated datasets with the observed datasets shows how well or poorly the model captures the essential characteristics of the data.

Prior predictive checks simulate data directly from the prior, in the absense of any observed data. The resulting datasets, often called y_sim, instead of y_rep, show the possible range of data that is consistent with the priors. This can be used to diagnose priors which are too strong or too weak.

The Stan User’s Guide shows how to code in order to check all priors. Unlike posterior predictive checks, in order to efficiently do the simulation, it is necessary to rewrite the model. In this notebook, we only want to verify that the BYM2 model does in fact properly scale the variance of phi, so we only need to simulate the convolved spatial and random effects component gamma, which will allow us to check theta, phi, and rho.

Checking effect of scaling phi by tau.

To examine the effect of the scaling factor, we simulate the parameters gamma, phi, theta, and rho using a simplified version of the model that excludes both the observed data (y and xs) and the Poisson regression component. This allows us to assess the resulting priors on phi, theta, and rho before incorporating any data.

Python

bym2_gamma_ppc_file = os.path.join('stan', 'bym2_gamma_ppc.stan')
with open(bym2_gamma_ppc_file, 'r') as file:
    contents = file.read()
    print(contents)

R

bym2_gamma_ppc_file = file.path('stan', 'bym2_gamma_ppc.stan')
cat(readLines(bym2_gamma_ppc_file), sep="\n")
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  // spatial structure
  int<lower = 0> N_edges;  // number of neighbor pairs
  array[2, N_edges] int<lower = 1, upper = N> neighbors;  // columnwise adjacent

  real tau; // scaling factor
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> rho; // proportion of spatial variance
  sum_to_zero_vector[N] phi;  // spatial effects
  vector[N] theta; // heterogeneous random effects
  real<lower = 0> sigma;  // scale of combined effects
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] gamma = sqrt(1 - rho) * theta + sqrt(rho * inv(tau)) * phi;  // BYM2
}
model {
  rho ~ beta(0.5, 0.5);
  target += -0.5 * dot_self(phi[neighbors[1]] - phi[neighbors[2]]); // ICAR prior
  theta ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ std_normal();
}

Model compilation

Python

bym2_gamma_ppc_mod = CmdStanModel(stan_file=bym2_gamma_ppc_file)

R

bym2_gamma_ppc_mod = cmdstan_model(stan_file=bym2_gamma_ppc_file)

Run model, check variances

In the BYM2 model, phi is scaled by the square root of \(1\)/tau since the ICAR component phi follows a multivariate normal distribution with covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), whereas theta is a vector of standard normal variables.

Python

bym2_gamma_ppc_fit = bym2_gamma_ppc_mod.sample(data = bym2_data)
phi = bym2_gamma_ppc_fit.stan_variable('phi')  # shape (n_draws, N)
phi_var_by_region = np.var((np.sqrt(1/tau) * phi), axis=0)  # variance across draws for each region
print('mean variance of phi scaled', np.mean(phi_var_by_region))

theta = bym2_gamma_ppc_fit.stan_variable('theta')  # shape (n_draws, N)
print('mean variance of theta', np.mean(np.var(theta, axis=0)))

R

bym2_gamma_ppc_fit = bym2_gamma_ppc_mod$sample(data=bym2_data, parallel_chains=cores, refresh=0)

print(paste("mean variance of phi scaled:", mean(phi_var_by_region)))
[1] "mean variance of phi scaled: 1.05630833594757"
theta <- as_draws_matrix(bym2_gamma_ppc_fit$draws("theta"))

print(paste("mean variance of theta:", mean(theta_var_by_region)))

Check rho

The fitted model also provides an estimate of rho, which has prior

rho ~ beta(0.5, 0.5);

As expected, before seeing any data, the value of rho matches the prior.

Python

rho = bym2_gamma_ppc_fit.stan_variable('rho')
print('mean rho', np.mean(rho))

R

rho <- as_draws_array(bym2_gamma_ppc_fit$draws("rho"))
mean(rho)

Comparison with the Leroux model

When the scaling factor tau is 1.0, the BYM2 model is equivalent to the Leroux model, and in this case, we can compute the variance of phi directly.

print(paste("mean variance of phi:", mean(apply(phi, 2, var))))

Model Checking

Visualizing the ICAR component

To see the spatial structure of the data, we plot the covariance matrix of phi. We expect neighboring regions to be correlated, and distant regions to be uncorrelated. To do this, we have written a helper function, plot_icar_corr_matrix, which plots just the upper half of the correlation matrix of phi, with red indicating positive correlation and blue indicating negative correlation. The census tracts are listed roughly in geographic order, from north-to-south and east-to-west, thus adjacent elements along the diagonal are spatially adjacent.

Python

phi_bym2 = bym2_fit.stan_variable("phi")
corr_plot = plot_icar_corr_matrix(phi_bym2, 'BYM2 spatial correlation', (10, 10))
corr_plot

R

phi_bym2 <- as_draws_matrix(bym2_fit$draws("phi"))
plot_icar_corr_matrix(phi_bym2, 'BYM2 spatial correlation')
Comparison to simple ICAR model

Python

pois_icar_mod = CmdStanModel(stan_file=os.path.join(
  'stan', 'poisson_icar.stan'))
pois_icar_fit = pois_icar_mod.sample(data=bym2_data)
phi_icar = pois_icar_fit.stan_variable("phi")
corr_plot = plot_icar_corr_matrix(phi_icar, 'ICAR spatial correlation', (10, 10))
corr_plot

R

pois_icar_mod = cmdstan_model(stan_file=file.path(
  'stan', 'poisson_icar.stan')) 
pois_icar_fit = pois_icar_mod$sample(data=bym2_data, parallel_chains=cores, refresh=0)

Compared to the covariance matrix of phi for the BYM2 model, the spatial correlations are less sharp, i.e. the addition of component theta allows phi to more strongly identify the spatial correlation structure of the data.

Compare overall variance

In the these models sigma determines the overall magnitude of variation in the combined spatial (phi) and non-spatial(theta) random effects. The BYM2 model adds parameter rho, the proportion of variance which is spatially structured.

Python

print('BYM2')
print(bym2_summary.round(2).loc[['sigma', 'rho']])

print('\nPoisson ICAR')
print(pois_icar_summary.round(2).loc[['sigma']])

print('\nPoisson Ordinary random effects')
print(pois_re_summary.round(2).loc[['sigma']])

Discussion

The BYM2 model and the Poisson + RE model provide similar estimates; however the BYM2 model provides additional information about the spatial vs. non-spatial structure of the variance.
